strengths: L4Q addresses a relevant NLP deployment problem: combining inexpensive adaptation with low-bit inference. Quantizing the merged base weights and LoRA update provides a clear route to removing the separate high-precision adapter path.

The evaluation spans OpenLLaMA, LLaMA-1/2, and Mistral models from 3B to 33B parameters, with both 3-bit and 4-bit results. Several improvements are substantial: for example, 3-bit LLaMA-2 7B commonsense accuracy reaches 61.3%, versus 57.6% for QLoRA*.

The paper reports practical resource measurements alongside accuracy. For 7B models, reported training memory is 25.4 GB, close to LoRA's 25.1 GB and substantially below the QAT baseline's 79.5 GB. Measurements using an inference kernel support the benefit of eliminating the adapter branch.
The initialization, rank, and quantization-group ablations provide useful implementation guidance. The appendices also supply task-level results and substantial experimental detail.
weaknesses: The custom backward derivation needs correction and verification. Equations (29)–(30) attach a weight-shaped clipping condition to adapter-shaped gradients. With G = dL/dWq and elementwise mask M = 1[QN <= w <= QP], the gradients should be alpha B^T(G ⊙ M) and alpha(G ⊙ M)A^T. Masking must occur before these matrix products. The manuscript does not establish whether this is only a notation error or affects the implementation; verification against an explicit STE autograd reference is needed.

The explanation of the memory advantage is insufficiently established. Intermediate weight gradients need not persist across all layers in frozen-weight QAT-LoRA; local disposal and recomputation are applicable there too. A saved-tensor memory breakdown and a QAT-LoRA baseline with the same memory optimizations would distinguish the contribution of quantization placement from implementation choices. Likewise, QAT-LoRA's parameter updates already interact through the shared loss, so describing them as inherently decoupled overstates the mechanism argument.

The efficiency comparisons contain an important confound. Appendix D specifies sequence length 128 only for L4Q on the 33B model, versus 2048 for the other settings, undermining direct comparisons of training memory and time. Comparable total training time also relies on giving L4Q half as many iterations; one training-loss curve does not establish comparable time to a validated target quality. Matched sequence lengths and validation-based convergence measurements are needed.

Baseline evidence supports narrower claims than the paper makes. Replacing QLoRA and LoftQ's quantizers with uniform quantization provides useful hardware control, but establishes comparisons against modified variants. The near-chance 3-bit LoftQ* MMLU results require diagnosis, particularly because its training settings are incomplete. A baseline that fine-tunes LoRA, merges it, and then applies PTQ would also directly test the benefit of joint QAT under the same final inference format.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the detailed appendices. Microbatch size, gradient accumulation, checkpointing, LoRA scaling, and several baseline settings are unspecified. Figure 3 reports 100 training steps while Appendix B reports 12,800 iterations with batch size 128; the units need reconciliation. Only upstream framework repositories are linked, leaving the custom implementation unavailable to resolve these ambiguities.

Several leading accuracy margins are only 0.1–0.3 percentage points, without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates. Superiority is also not universal: on 3-bit LLaMA-2 13B MMLU 5-shot, L4Q scores 50.0% versus QLoRA*'s 50.6%. The promising results warrant further consideration, but the backward-pass specification and uncontrolled resource comparisons require important, plausibly next-cycle revisions before a sound and reproducible Findings recommendation.
